title: Walk through the 10-step Spark execution lifecycle: (1) Driver starts SparkSession, (2) Cluster Manager provisions Executors, (3) DAG built from transformations, (4) Catalyst Optimizer builds logical→physical plan (for DataFrames/SQL), (5) DAGScheduler creates Stages at shuffle boundaries, (6) TaskScheduler creates Tasks (one per partition per stage), (7) Executors run Tasks in parallel, (8) Shuffle exchanges data between stages, (9) Results returned to Driver or written to storage, (10) SparkSession.stop() releases resources.

s1_definition.profdef: The Spark execution lifecycle is the ordered sequence by which a Spark application runs. The Driver starts a SparkSession, the Cluster Manager provisions Executors, transformations build a logical DAG, the Catalyst optimizer turns the logical plan into an optimized physical plan for DataFrames and SQL, the DAGScheduler splits the job into stages at shuffle boundaries, the TaskScheduler creates one task per partition per stage, executors run those tasks in parallel, shuffles exchange data between stages, results are returned to the Driver or written to storage, and finally stopping the SparkSession releases all resources.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India launching a big reporting project. The manager opens the project office (SparkSession). HR assigns desks and clerks (Executors). The manager writes the plan of steps (the DAG). A consultant reorders and streamlines the plan to be efficient (Catalyst). The plan is cut into phases wherever paperwork must be re-sorted between teams (stages at shuffle boundaries). Each phase is broken into one task per box of files (tasks). Clerks do the tasks in parallel. Between phases, files are re-sorted and handed over (shuffle). The finished report is handed to the manager or filed in the vault (results). Finally the project office is closed and desks are freed (stop).
s1_definition.oneliner: Session start, executor provisioning, DAG build, Catalyst optimization, stage splitting at shuffles, one task per partition, parallel execution, shuffle exchange, results out, and session stop — that is the full Spark lifecycle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Spark execution lifecycle is the ordered sequence by which a Spark application runs. The Driver starts a SparkSession, the Cluster Manager provisions Executors, transformations build a logical DAG, the Catalyst optimizer turns the logical plan into an optimized physical plan for DataFrames and SQL, the DAGScheduler splits the job into stages at shuffle boundaries, the TaskScheduler creates one task per partition per stage, executors run those tasks in parallel, shuffles exchange data between stages, results are returned to the Driver or written to storage, and finally stopping the SparkSession releases all resources.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India launching a big reporting project. The manager opens the project office (SparkSession). HR assigns desks and clerks (Executors). The manager writes the plan of steps (the DAG). A consultant reorders and streamlines the plan to be efficient (Catalyst). The plan is cut into phases wherever paperwork must be re-sorted between teams (stages at shuffle boundaries). Each phase is broken into one task per box of files (tasks). Clerks do the tasks in parallel. Between phases, files are re-sorted and handed over (shuffle). The finished report is handed to the manager or filed in the vault (results). Finally the project office is closed and desks are freed (stop).

**One line to remember:** Session start, executor provisioning, DAG build, Catalyst optimization, stage splitting at shuffles, one task per partition, parallel execution, shuffle exchange, results out, and session stop — that is the full Spark lifecycle.

sections.s2_technical:
Steps one and two set up the application. Creating a SparkSession starts the Driver, which is the master process holding your program, the DAG, and the schedulers. The Driver then negotiates with the Cluster Manager — Standalone, YARN, Kubernetes, or a managed service — which provisions Executors on worker nodes with the requested cores and memory. These executors are long-lived and will run all the tasks for the application.

Steps three and four build and optimize the plan. As you call transformations like filter, select, and join, Spark records them into a logical DAG rather than executing them, because transformations are lazy. For DataFrames and SQL, when an action triggers execution, the Catalyst optimizer takes over: it parses the logical plan, analyzes it against the schema, applies optimizations like predicate pushdown and column pruning to the logical plan, and then produces a physical plan, often with whole-stage code generation that compiles operators into tight JVM bytecode.

Steps five and six schedule the work. The DAGScheduler walks the plan and cuts it into stages wherever there is a wide dependency, because a shuffle is a hard boundary that the next stage must wait for. Within each stage, the TaskScheduler creates tasks following the one-task-per-partition-per-stage rule and assigns them to executor cores, respecting data locality where possible. Steps seven and eight do the computation: executors run the tasks in parallel, and between stages a shuffle exchanges data across the network — each task of the earlier stage writes bucketed output to local disk and each task of the later stage reads the buckets it needs.

Steps nine and ten finish the application. When all stages complete, the action's result either returns to the Driver, as count returns a number or collect returns a list, or is written to storage, as write saves Parquet. Finally, stopping the SparkSession tells the Cluster Manager to release the executors and frees all resources. A senior nuance is that each action triggers its own run through steps three to nine against the current plan, so a job with multiple actions goes through the scheduling phases multiple times unless intermediate results are cached. Understanding this lifecycle is what lets you read the Spark UI — jobs map to actions, stages map to shuffle boundaries, and tasks map to partitions — and diagnose exactly where a banking job spends its time.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A big reporting job needs a clear, ordered path from "I wrote some transformations" to "the report is written." This is exactly the ten-step lifecycle.

Problem 2 — The job must be cut into phases wherever data is re-sorted, and each phase split into parallel units. This is exactly stage splitting at shuffle boundaries and one task per partition.

Problem 3 — At the end, resources must be released cleanly. This is exactly SparkSession stop.

The mini-project simulates the lifecycle in Java. A `SparkLifecycle` orchestrator runs ten clearly labelled steps: start session, provision executors, build the DAG, optimize it, split into stages at a shuffle, create tasks per partition, run tasks in parallel, perform the shuffle, return results, and stop. It processes Rajesh's and Priya's transactions, with a filter-and-map narrow phase and a groupBy wide phase so there is a real shuffle boundary and two stages.

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the lifecycle demo
java -cp target/spark-lifecycle-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.lifecycle.LifecycleDemo

# Reference: the real submission that triggers this lifecycle
spark-submit --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster \
  --num-executors 3 --executor-cores 2 --executor-memory 4g \
  --class com.bank.NightlyReportJob report.jar
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transactions in two partitions — partition 0 has Rajesh Rs.1000 and Priya Rs.500, partition 1 has Rajesh Rs.3000 and Priya Rs.700.

Step 1: The Driver starts the SparkSession; the master process is now alive and holds the plan and schedulers.

Step 2: The Cluster Manager provisions two executor cores, modelled as a thread pool, ready to run tasks.

Step 3 and 4: The DAG is built from the transformations filter, map, and groupBy, and Catalyst conceptually optimizes it with predicate pushdown and column pruning before producing a physical plan.

Step 5 and 6: The DAGScheduler splits the job into stage one, the narrow filter-and-map plus map-side combine, and stage two, the post-shuffle aggregation, with the boundary at the groupBy shuffle. The TaskScheduler creates two tasks for stage one, one per partition.

Step 7 and 8: The two stage-one tasks run in parallel, each producing local partials — partition 0 gives Rajesh Rs.1000 and Priya Rs.500, partition 1 gives Rajesh Rs.3000 and Priya Rs.700. The shuffle then merges partials by key into the stage-two buckets.

Step 9 and 10: The merged result, Rajesh Rs.4000 and Priya Rs.1200, is returned to the Driver, and the SparkSession is stopped, releasing the executors. The report is complete.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Spark execution lifecycle is a clear ten-step sequence, and being able to walk through it shows you understand how Spark actually runs. It begins when the Driver starts a SparkSession, which brings up the master process that holds the program, the DAG, and the schedulers. Next, the Cluster Manager — whether Standalone, YARN, Kubernetes, or a managed platform — provisions executors on worker nodes with the requested cores and memory. As I write transformations, Spark builds a logical DAG lazily, and when an action fires, the Catalyst optimizer turns that logical plan into an optimized physical plan for DataFrames and SQL, applying predicate pushdown, column pruning, and whole-stage code generation.

From there, the DAGScheduler splits the job into stages, cutting a new stage wherever there is a wide dependency, because a shuffle is a boundary the next stage must wait for. The TaskScheduler then creates tasks following the one-task-per-partition-per-stage rule and assigns them to executor cores with data locality in mind. The executors run the tasks in parallel, and between stages a shuffle exchanges data across the network, with earlier-stage tasks writing bucketed output and later-stage tasks reading the buckets they need. Finally, the action's result is either returned to the Driver or written to storage, and stopping the SparkSession tells the Cluster Manager to release the executors.

In my project at the National Bank of India this lifecycle was exactly how I read the Spark UI to diagnose slow jobs. Jobs in the UI correspond to actions, stages correspond to shuffle boundaries, and tasks correspond to partitions, so when a nightly report was slow I could pinpoint whether the cost was in a particular shuffle-heavy stage or in skewed tasks within a stage. One nuance I always mention is that each action triggers its own pass through the planning and execution steps, so a job with several actions repeats the scheduling phases unless I cache the shared intermediate result. Knowing this lifecycle end to end is what turned vague performance complaints into targeted fixes.
